source.title: Sparsity and Superposition in Mixture of Experts
source.authors: Marmik Chaudhari; Jeremi Nuer; Rome Thorstenson

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper extends toy superposition experiments to mixture-of-experts models, measuring feature norms, interference, and representation strategies across sparsity, importance, and expert-count conditions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results measuring superposition and feature allocation in toy models. It also reports reconstruction loss and expert-usage statistics relevant to feature allocation. It does not provide results on large language models or SAE feature completeness.
record.test_reason: The study re-runs the original toy-model superposition setup on dense models as comparators and replicates the phase change. It then applies the same norm, interference, dimensionality and phase-diagram measures to a new setting, toy mixture-of-experts autoencoders. Those results bear on V1 (superposition and sparsity-dependent transitions) and V2 (capacity and importance-driven allocation).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that toy MoEs show less superposition (more monosemanticity) than dense models with matched parameters. They find no discrete phase changes, with network sparsity rather than feature sparsity or importance governing representation. Experts specialize around coherent features when initialization encourages it. They claim comparable loss with more interpretable representations, though Appendix A.1 shows dense models keep lower loss. Transfer to large transformers is stated as uncertain.
record.recipe_differences: Extends the Toy Models of Superposition framework to synthetic MoE autoencoders, with expert routing and network-sparsity comparisons; it uses related feature-norm and interference measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Representation patterns vary with network sparsity, feature sparsity, relative feature importance, architecture, and router initialization. The paper reports a mixed feature-sparsity region around 0.48–0.7 in some MoE settings.

fits_no_version.finding: In toy MoEs, experts are used far more when the features they represent monosemantically are active. For k-hot initialization, usage reaches 100% when only those features are active (Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In toy MoEs, routing occupancy of a feature direction correlates with the expert representing that feature with low superposition.

record.problems: All experiments use controlled toy models with synthetic independent features. The paper notes that transfer to real MoE transformers is uncertain; it does not evaluate downstream performance trade-offs or behavior at scale. Many plotted phase-diagram values are not numerically reported in the text, and cells use the lowest-loss model among ten trained models.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted Appendix A.1 loss-sweep values and Appendix A.4 routing/loss examples because they concern reconstruction or routing performance rather than a direct measurement of feature superposition or the feature-allocation claims catalogued here. Figure 8's loss and variance results are also not included for the same reason.

untested.parts: Regular geometry (polytope or antipodal structures) is only mentioned in a footnote, not measured. Near-orthogonality is shown only in small Gram-matrix figures.
Neuron-level polysemanticity is not measured. The paper says 'monosemantic' means less superposition, not basis-aligned neurons.
Not tested; no LLM or SAE results.
Not tested; features are 1-D by construction.

missing.what: Efficient packing: summed feature dimensionality ≈ E·m for MoEs and ≈ m for dense ('Empirically, we find that both dense and MoE models satisfy'). Text only, no numbers.
In every E=2 MoE phase diagram, one expert specializes monosemantically in the most important feature.
Dense model represents 10 features versus 8 for the MoE at equal total parameters (Fig 1a vs 2a).

record.verdict_notes: Tranche T3: the MoE is a new setting, and the dense comparators are T1-style replications. The text is inconsistent on load balancing. Section 4.1 both adds and 'deliberately omits' it in 'Section 4'; Section 5 uses it; the limitations say none was used. The paper's 'monosemantic' means low superposition, not neuron basis-alignment, which limits the bearing on neuron-level V2. Several Table 1 categories rest on one or zero experts. Phase-diagram cells use the lowest-loss model of ten runs.

versions.untested_parts: The paper studies synthetic toy models, not learned representations in LLMs. Its MoE results are an extension of the dense toy-model setting.
It measures feature representation and expert usage in toy models, not polysemanticity of individual neurons in trained language models.
It does not test whether polysemanticity arises for reasons other than capacity pressure.
No LLM activation-spreading or SAE-recovery results are reported.
The paper does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
The toy setup represents each synthetic input feature by a vector, but does not test whether learned features in general are intrinsically one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

source_check.reason: Dense comparators exhibit feature interference, more features than dimensions and clear phase changes (r1, r3, r7, r9, r12).
